UNDER SECTION 206 OF THE FEDERAL POWER ACT  
AND CONSOLIDATING WITH OTHER PROCEEDINGS

Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 the Indicated PJM Transmission 
Owners, comprised of the majority of the named respondents and inclusive of investor-owned 
utilities, municipalities, and cooperatives (hereinafter, “Indicated TOs”)2 submit this unified

Answer to the Commission’s Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal 
Power Act3 and Consolidating with Other Proceedings, issued on February 20, 2025.4  The 
Indicated TOs support co-location and appreciate the Commission’s leadership in addressing this 
issue.  It is vital to our national economy and energy security to ensure that the rules of the road 
are clear with respect to the interconnection, service, and cost allocation for co-located 
arrangements.   
Co-located load can and does fit within the current constructs for providing transmission 
service under the Commission’s pro forma open access transmission tariff (“OATT”) and PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”).  The 
existing PJM Tariff provisions are just and reasonable.  The Indicated TOs appreciate that further 
clarification of how those existing provisions apply to co-located load arrangements could be 
beneficial for all parties involved in those arrangements and the industry as a whole.  Thus, the 
Indicated TOs support the Commission ruling, as part of its review in this proceeding, that the 
existing PJM Tariff and its existing two forms of transmission service—Network Integration 
Transmission Service (“Network Service”) and Point-to-Point Transmission Service (“Point-to-
Point Service”)5—encompass and apply to these arrangements.  
 
Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative, Inc.; UGI Utilities Inc; and Wabash Valley Power Association, Inc.

I. 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
The Indicated TOs agree with the recommendation of PJM that co-located end-use loads 
should be treated as load in front of the meter and designated as Network Load.6  Co-located load 
should be treated as load in front of the meter and designated as Network Load because it will 
ensure that such loads are appropriately studied, charged, and factored in operationally by PJM 
and transmission owners.  Doing otherwise would undercut reliability and exacerbate 
affordability concerns.  This approach offers the most reliability benefits and a cost allocation 
framework that addresses charges for use of, and reliance on, the transmission system.  
Otherwise, a customer that co-locates avoids “wires charges”—the fixed costs of the poles, 
wires, transformers, and substations that comprise the transmission and distribution network.  
These avoided costs are then subsidized by other customers, allowing co-location customers a 
free ride.  Beneficiaries of the transmission system must pay their share to avoid inappropriately 
shifting costs to other customers.   
PJM’s Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) has correctly submitted that “it is simply 
not possible to be off the grid if you are interconnected to the grid.”7  The North American 
Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) recognized in its 2024 Long-Term Reliability 
Assessment (“2024 LTRA”) that, in PJM, “[t]he trends in demand growth and resource additions 
create resource adequacy and system planning challenges for PJM as it carefully manages 
generator deactivation requests from the aging fossil and nuclear fleet.”8  PJM is experiencing

increased load growth.9  NERC has also explained that there are reliability challenges that attend 
this demand growth: 
PJM’s 2023 Load Forecast Report addressed the impact of industry 
changes that are reshaping system hourly loads.  As a result, the 
level and timing of coincident peak and non-coincident peak 
demands across PJM have begun to shift.  Solar-power penetration, 
expected impacts of EVs, state electrification programs, home 
battery storage, and a significant increase in data center loads are 
markedly increasing the complexity of PJM’s load forecasting 
process.  Driven by discrete and localized load growth, like Data 
Center Alley in Loudoun County, Virginia, in 2022, PJM and 
stakeholders conducted a review of data center load growth and 
identified growth rates of over 300% in some instances.  As a result, 
the 2023 PJM Load Forecast Report incorporates adjustments to 
specific zones for data center load growth.10 
 
The foregoing underscores the importance of ensuring that when there are co-location 
arrangements that must rely on the transmission system, and receive system benefits, for any 
period of time, the loads should be located and treated just like load in front of the meter and 
designated as Network Load so that their demand is transparent and known, so that they can be 
charged the costs commensurate with the benefits they are receiving, and to ensure PJM and 
transmission owners are adequately studying the load to ensure effective system planning. 
The concept of placing end-use load near generation, and vice versa, is not new.  As 
industry analysts have recognized, new large loads located at generating facilities are seeking 
ways to interconnect to the PJM system faster than current process timelines for addressing the 
generation and transmission needs of the system.  The Indicated TOs recognize that FERC, PJM,

Assessment_2024.pdf.

Loudoun County, Virginia, in the PJM assessment area, is home to ‘Data Center Alley,’ the largest concentration of 
data centers in the world. Electrification in transportation, heating, and industrial sectors is also spurring demand

and stakeholders are working diligently and are in the process of implementing queue reforms 
and proposals to address bringing needed capacity online to serve the increased demand. 
Co-location can offer a valuable option for hyperscalers to address transmission capacity 
constraints and to spur economic growth.  The contractual arrangement between a generator and 
co-located load also has the potential to provide generation assets an alternative to retirement.  
However, co-location must be done in a responsible and fair manner to ensure configurations do 
not threaten the reliability and security of the grid,11 and co-location should not result in other 
cost-shifting that requires customers to pay costs caused by or for the benefit of co-location 
customers.  If co-located load is interconnected to the transmission system, it is unequivocally 
using and benefitting from the transmission system and therefore must pay for its share of 
wholesale transmission service and other essential grid services. 
This is the case regardless of whether the load contracts for power directly from a 
generator connected to the PJM transmission system.  The transmission system must be planned 
and built to support every MW of load on the system, including co-located load.  Co-located load 
depends on and uses the grid.  As stated above, if the framework for cost allocation for the 
transmission system does not reflect co-located load’s use of the system, then such co-located 
load will get a free ride, and costs will be shifted to and borne by other customers.  
Consequently, the Commission should confirm that the existing PJM Tariff provisions regarding 
Network Service and Point-to-Point Service are sufficiently inclusive to cover the treatment of 
co-located load.   
 
11 Should behind-the-meter co-location configurations be permitted even when such configurations depend on the 
transmission system, there will be reliability and resource adequacy risks that will follow.  As the Commission 
recognized in its Show Cause Order, “[t]he risk that co-located loads will not be reflected in resource adequacy 
planning mechanisms with sufficient forward notice is particularly concerning given how long it takes to add new 
generation capacity or upgrade transmission facilities.”  Show Cause Order at P 85.

6 
 
That said, as the Commission has acknowledged, co-located load arrangements are 
becoming increasingly common in PJM,12 in part due to variations to the Commission’s pro 
forma OATT that are specific to PJM.  Thus, the time is ripe to underscore and clarify the 
applicability of the existing types of PJM transmission service to co-location arrangements to 
provide certainty to participants in those arrangements and other stakeholders, ensure that the 
Commission’s principles for open access and non-discriminatory transmission service persist, 
and that beneficiaries pay for the services they receive.  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission also instructed PJM and the Indicated TOs to 
file responses to a list of questions, together with supporting evidence and analysis.13  Thus, 
along with the fundamental principles and arguments raised herein, the Indicated TOs submit 
answers to the questions in Attachment A of this filing.14  
II. 
BACKGROUND 
A. Procedural Overview 
The Show Cause Order is the culmination of several proceedings addressing the issue of 
co-location, both in specific circumstances and on an industry-wide basis.  The Commission 
consolidated this new proceeding in Docket No. EL25-49-000 with Docket Nos. AD24-11-000 
(the co-location technical conference) and EL25-20-000 (the “Complaint”).15  While the co-
location phenomenon is not limited to a single region, the Show Cause Order is specific and 
limited to PJM.  In its Show Cause Order, the Commission directed the respondents to:

B. Co-location of Load 
Co-located load is network or point-to-point load that has contractual arrangements to be 
served by an adjacent generation resource that is physically interconnected to and synchronized 
with the transmission and/or distribution grid.  Indeed, it must be interconnected to the grid.17  
Co-located load uses and depends on the grid, causing changing flows on the grid from second to 
second.  There is an alternative arrangement where a load and accompanying generation never 
use the transmission or distribution system—they are islanded—but neither the Show Cause 
Order nor Commission jurisdiction extend to islanded non-interconnected arrangements.  Load 
cannot be both connected to the transmission and/or distribution grid and “fully isolated,” in the 
manner certain generation and large load interests have asserted.18 
 
16 Id. at P 2. 
17 FERC adopts the definition of a co-located load arrangement used in PJM’s Guidance Document for purposes of 
the Show Cause Order: “A co-located load configuration refers to end-use customer load that is physically 
connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the Interconnection Customer’s side of the 
Point of Interconnection (‘POI’) to the PJM Transmission System (co-located Customer Facility).”  Show Cause 
Order at P 3 n.4.  This definition obscures the engineering and economic truth that the load relies upon the

and appropriate cost allocation.

Throughout the proceedings leading up to this Show Cause Order, several parties argued 
that co-located load could be “fully isolated” by connecting with their own generation and 
therefore not relying on the transmission grid.19  Connecting the load near generation with which

from the grid.  It continues to use services provided by the grid and the arrangement continues to 
rely on the grid connection for the generator to operate.  As long as the load remains connected 
to the grid, including through facilities also connecting a generator to the grid, the load would 
still be able to be served from the transmission system, and therefore, the transmission system 
must be planned and built to account for the load.  The fact that the load is not constant does not 
reduce the capital investment or operation and maintenance costs that are incurred to ensure that 
the system is available to the customer.  The same applies to generators connected to the 
distribution system.

Indeed, any characterization of co-located load as “fully isolated” is false and misleading 
unless the load is not connected to either the transmission or distribution system.  If loads were 
“fully isolated” from the grid, then both the generation and the load would be islanded from the 
grid, and the PJM Tariff would not apply to them at all.  No interconnection under the PJM 
Tariff process would be needed.  The Indicated TOs consider all the arrangements being 
contemplated or requested as being interconnected with and synchronized with the transmission 
and/or distribution grid and thus not “fully isolated.”   
Although the existing PJM Tariff already accommodates co-located load, the 
Commission may have an interest in providing further clarity.  If so, a definition of “co-located 
load” could be added to the PJM Tariff that clarifies the expectations and obligations associated 
with such load.  Specifically, the Indicated TOs suggest that the following definition could be 
added to the PJM Tariff:  
“Co-located Load” shall mean load that has contractual 
arrangements to be served by an adjacent generation resource that is 
physically interconnected to and synchronized with the transmission 
or distribution grid.  Co-located Load is either Network Load or load 
being served using Point-to-Point Transmission Service, as 
applicable.  Such adjacent generation resource shall not meet the 
definition of Behind The Meter Generation.  Arrangements for Co-
located Load must have separate metering for load consumption and 
generator output as required under PJM Tariff, Part III.   
 
This proposed definition is consistent with the provisions of the existing PJM Tariff but 
would provide additional clarity to those directly impacted by co-located load arrangements.  At 
the same time, this proposed language would ensure that PJM and its transmission owners have 
adequate visibility of the loads affecting the transmission system for planning and reliability 
purposes.

10 
 
III. 
DISCUSSION 
A. Classification of Co-located Load as Network Load Is Just and Reasonable. 
The PJM Tariff, in its current form, allows for co-location of load and generation on 
terms that are just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  The PJM Tariff 
allows end-use load and generation to co-locate expeditiously and on terms that are also fair to 
all other users of the grid and commensurate with cost causation principles.  To allow this, the 
PJM Tariff, consistent with the pro forma OATT, provides for two types of transmission service 
to be used in accommodating co-location arrangements: Network Service and Point-to-Point 
Service.  Both long-standing types of transmission service recognize that those that benefit from 
the transmission system must contribute to its costs.  
The rate design in PJM, incorporated into the PJM Tariff, permits owners to recover, on a 
postage stamp basis without consideration of the distance between load and generation, the 
embedded costs of their respective portions of the transmission grid from network customers.20  
As the Commission has explained, “PJM recovers the full revenue requirements of existing 
facilities (embedded costs) through its firm transmission rates.”21   
This concept of embedded costs of the transmission grid and associated cost 
responsibility of load based on fairness principles predates Order No. 888,22 FERC’s landmark

The existing PJM Tariff is just and reasonable.  With that said, the Indicated TOs remain 
open to and anticipate the potential for further discussion regarding possible changes to tariffs to 
expressly specify that co-located load must be served by the existing forms of transmission 
service—Network Service or Point-to-Point Service—while recognizing the evolving co-location

B. Co-Located Load Benefits From Essential Services Provided Using the Grid. 
In addition to FERC-jurisdictional transmission charges, PJM also assesses service 
charges to users of the grid for essential reliability services, such as ancillary services.  As PJM 
acknowledged, there is no question that “[a]lthough co-located load is located behind the [point 
of interconnection], it still is electrically connected and synchronized to the PJM Transmission 
System when consuming power and therefore benefits from the use of the Transmission System 
and Ancillary Services.”27  The same is true even when the co-located load is only connected to 
the distribution system, because ancillary services are required by both the transmission and 
distribution system operators to maintain the integrity and stability of the transmission and 
distribution system, as well as the power quality.28  In other words, co-located load cannot 
receive the benefits of such essential reliability services without the physical and synchronous 
interconnection to the transmission (and/or distribution) system.  These services are fundamental

should be treated like any other load.  Because the co-located load is interconnected with the grid 
and relies on the grid, PJM’s Tariff remains just and reasonable.  The PJM Tariff currently

It is undeniable that the synchronized configurations associated with co-located load 
benefit from essential reliability services provided by the regional PJM grid.29  By way of 
example: load served by a nuclear unit necessarily depends on a grid interconnection because the 
nuclear unit is not permitted by its license to operate without a robust grid interconnection.30  
Further, load that is co-located with a nuclear unit depends on services such as load following, 
voltage support, black start, and other ancillary services that will be and can only be delivered 
over the grid.31  Nuclear units cannot move their output up and down from moment to moment to 
match variations in the load, and because the nuclear units cannot provide these services, they 
must instead be provided through connection to the grid.32  That is, remote generators increase 
and decrease their output in synchrony with the co-located load, and power flows on the grid 
likewise move in synchrony with the co-located demand.  Those services are used every hour,

Because these arrangements irrefutably rely on the transmission grid, there can be no 
need for some new kind of service for these arrangements.  The PJM Tariff already has 
mechanisms that lay out how transmission users connect loads—those mechanisms work.  Any 
proposed tariff changes to be considered by the Indicated TOs as part of a separate process

to co-located load; the fundamental principles established by the PJM Tariff cover co-location

C. All Load, Including Co-located Load, Is Used to Plan the Transmission 
System.

Treating co-located end-use load like all other end-use load on the system by requiring it to take 
Network Service or Point-to-Point Service avoids the need to modify the capacity market rules 
and ensures that those rules are not unduly discriminatory or preferential against any customer.  
To be clear, and as discussed above, the PJM RAA requires all LSEs in PJM to subject

between specific generating units and load customers.  Those rules work for co-located load and 
its relationship to the co-located generator as long as the load is treated as a Network Customer.  
This straightforward approach to handling co-located load with regard to the capacity market has 
the considerable benefit of not requiring changes to PJM’s capacity market.  The broader 
circumstances and challenges currently facing PJM’s capacity market would not benefit from 
further intervention and reform due to co-located load arrangements at a time when there are 
considerable resource adequacy concerns in the PJM footprint and there are efforts being made 
to advance certainty in the capacity market design.

owner have sufficient visibility into the co-located load configuration?  
 
In general, changes to the applicable pro forma service agreements are not appropriate.  As long 
as co-located load is treated like all other load on the system, including as to metering and telemetry, 
and is a retail customer of the relevant distribution utility, the relevant state retail tariffs provide

18
 
the appropriate visibility into the co-located load configuration, just as they do for any other load 
interconnection. 
 
Interconnection agreements should include appropriate metering requirements. As stated above, 
co-located loads served from the transmission system under PJM Tariff, Part III, must have 
separate metering for load consumption and generator output. 
 
iii. 
Please explain whether the existing Tariff rules are sufficient to ensure 
resource adequacy if increasing numbers of large existing generators 
choose to co-locate with load; 
 
Adding load located at a generator site to the system, like adding any other new load, introduces 
challenges to the existing resource adequacy problem.  But as with other such load, existing PJM 
Tariff rules should be sufficient to study the impacts as long as co-located load is recognized as 
the load addition that it is, comparable to other new load additions to the system.  Co-located load 
designated as Network Load will be included in the load forecasts and will receive appropriate 
treatment in the capacity market auctions, as discussed above. 
 
iv. 
What deactivation or interconnection modification studies should PJM 
undertake to ensure resource adequacy and/or protect reliability should an 
existing generator seek to enter into a co-location arrangement?  If PJM 
finds that the co-location would cause reliability standards violations, what 
remediation techniques would be appropriate (e.g., reliability must-run 
contracts, delaying the co-location arrangement until the reliability 
violations are addressed, etc.)?  
 
Co-located end-use load should be studied under the relevant state jurisdictional process for new 
load additions and PJM’s role should be limited to the standard transmission planning process for 
all new load additions.  Additionally, the loss of capacity from an existing generator seeking to 
enter into a co-location arrangement should be studied by PJM.  Because the federal role in end-
use load additions is limited, PJM and the Commission should not create processes in the PJM 
Tariff that would interfere with state jurisdiction.  However, all load, and separately, all generation, 
that want to connect to the grid should go through the established PJM study processes to ensure 
the reliability of the grid.  As stated above, if an existing generator proposes modifications to 
enable it to operate in a co-located arrangement, then any transmission upgrades related to the 
generator modifications would need to be paid by that generator. 
 
v. 
What changes are necessary, if any, to other PJM planning processes to 
better plan for and address the resource adequacy and reliability impacts 
of co-location arrangements, including, for example, whether or not the

19
 
frequency of such processes might be changed?  Similarly, should PJM 
consider changes to load forecasting methods, informational postings, or 
the reserve margin study process to better plan for and address the 
resource adequacy and reliability impacts of co-location arrangements?   
 
All load additions create new demands for energy regardless of their location.  The resource 
adequacy and reliability challenges exist regardless of whether end-use load is connected to the 
grid at a generator site or elsewhere, and regardless of whether the point of connection lies “behind” 
or “in front of” the generator’s meter.  Changes to the planning and load forecasting processes 
should not be needed solely to address end-use load that is located at a generator as long as co-
located load is treated like all other load on the system and takes either Network Service or Point-
to-Point Service. 
 
vi. 
Under what circumstances can PJM direct the operators of co-location 
arrangements to shed such load if deemed necessary to preserve system 
reliability during a declared emergency? 
 
If treated as Network Load, co-located end-use load can only be shed by PJM when required under 
the relevant NERC and PJM standards as documented in PJM’s Manual 13 on Emergency 
Operations.  The general terms and conditions governing service to co-located end-use load are 
regulated by states, which are free to offer optional or mandatory interruptible service rates.   
 
We note that failure to meter the co-located load will lead to anomalous results.  For example, if 
the generator trips offline without disconnecting from the transmission system, the unmetered load 
“appears” on the system and draws power from the grid.  In an extreme case, this can create a 
system emergency that requires load drop—which must come from other network load that did 
not cause the emergency. 
 
f. Other  
i. 
Are any changes to PJM’s energy or ancillary services market rules 
necessary to address co-location arrangements? 
 
Other changes are not necessary.  If co-located end-use load is treated like all other end-use load 
on the system, served through either Network Service or Point-to-Point Service, there is no gap in 
the existing rules.   
 
ii. 
Please discuss whether back-up service can provide benefits to customers 
or otherwise help minimize system costs, including with specific examples 
or best practices, if possible;

20
 
In general, having reliable backup generation can benefit any end-use load by providing alternative 
sources of power in times of system emergency.  That capability can also benefit other end-use 
load customers if it can and is used for their benefit as well.  However, the presence of on-site 
backup generation does not exempt load from paying the costs of transmission service, because it 
still benefits from the transmission system.  It does not matter whether that load is co-located with 
generation.  Notably, nuclear units must be interconnected with the transmission grid to operate, 
so any backup service provided by a nuclear unit is dependent on continued grid operation to 
function at all. 
 
iii. 
Parties may also choose to address how co-location arrangements may 
provide benefits, including potentially reducing required transmission 
upgrades to interconnect large loads, reducing congestion, or providing 
operational flexibility during system peaks or emergencies?   
 
A study is necessary to determine, on a case-by-case basis, whether co-located load generally 
would result in a reduction of required transmission upgrades, reduction in congestion, or provide 
operational flexibility during system peaks or emergencies.  Thus, although the Indicated TOs 
recognize that there could be some instances in which co-location of load, like other load, may 
provide benefits to the transmission system, that cannot be determined until after full studies are 
completed.   
 
iv. 
Parties may also address whether, and if so, how, the Tariff should be 
modified to best accommodate or encourage co-location arrangements to 
be constructed in such a way as to minimize total system costs or 
otherwise provide certain benefits, including protections for existing 
customers and allocation of costs consistent with the cost-causation 
principle; 
 
No federal tariff changes are needed to promote co-location because the current PJM Tariff and 
state regulatory regimes can and do accommodate reliable and economic co-located configurations 
under existing rules.  If there is a hurdle to locating end-use load at generation sites, that hurdle is 
not the lack of a rate discount, but of confusion over the applicability of the established tariffs.  
The best way to ensure cost-effective co-location is to maintain consistent rules: treat co-located 
load as any other load on the system.  The Indicated TOs also note that states may choose to 
promote co-location arrangements through, for example, appropriate distribution tariffs or tax 
incentives—whether the states choose to do so is not within FERC’s jurisdiction or control.   
 
v. 
What Tariff provisions, if any, are necessary to ensure clarity regarding 
the aspects of service to co-located load and generation facilities that may 
be administered through the Tariff versus state jurisdictional retail tariffs?

21
 
 
Consistent with existing precedent, the Commission might clarify that generator interconnection 
agreements do not themselves provide for or confer the right to serve end-use retail load or the 
right of new load to take retail service at a specific point or under particular rates; instead, such 
services are regulated under state law.  Potential customers could benefit from clarification by the 
Commission that co-located load is Network Load and must be included in the load of either a 
Network Customer or arranged for Point-to-Point Service.  Alternatively, the Indicated TOs are 
open to working with PJM and other stakeholders to incorporate appropriate PJM Tariff revisions 
to expressly specify that co-located load must be served by the existing forms of transmission 
service—Network Service or Point-to-Point Service.   
 
vi. 
We also encourage parties to address any national security implications 
associated with co-location arrangements, including with respect to the 
specific issues discussed in this show cause order, and what actions, if 
any, the Commission should take in response. 
 
Allowing co-location arrangements to move forward rapidly and without regulatory ambiguity is 
the best way to achieve the national security goals of this Commission and this administration.  
The most straightforward way to accomplish that goal is simply to recognize that co-located load 
is Network Load like all other load on the system and should pay for Network Service like all other 
customers.  A clear statement from this Commission that the existing rules work, and that co-
located load can be served under existing rules is the fastest path to data center interconnections 
needed to win the artificial intelligence (AI) race.  In contrast, development of new forms of service, 
and efforts to mesh those new forms of service with the existing rules, will certainly get bogged 
down in extended litigation that will impede efforts to develop AI. 
 
Any delays associated with interconnection of co-located load experienced thus far have not been 
because the rates do not provide for artificial exemption of the arrangements from transmission 
rates, but because of efforts to dispute the applicability of those rates.  Importantly, this does not 
preclude PJM and the PJM TOs from considering and pursuing beneficial enhancements as the 
business areas surrounding co-location continue to evolve.  As previously noted, the Indicated TOs 
are attempting to consider potential beneficial enhancements collectively and with PJM, consistent 
with existing rights and responsibilities.    
 
vii. 
Finally, for generation units paid for originally by consumers in base rates 
prior to restructuring, is it fair and/or just and reasonable if these units are 
taken out of the system’s supply stack and devoted exclusively to serving 
co-location arrangements with one or a few large customers?

22
 
There are two issues here: generation costs and transmission costs.  In general, the continued 
obligation, if any, of generation to serve classes of end-use customers who pay for that generation 
is a matter of state jurisdiction and concern.  Transmission costs are certainly a matter of FERC 
concern.  The addition of end-use load, including co-located load, at established cost-based rates 
typically benefits other customers with respect to transmission costs, because the shared embedded 
costs of the grid are paid by all customers, so that new load additions spread those costs more 
broadly.  Treating co-located end-use load like all other load additions by requiring them to take 
either Network Service or Point-to-Point Service ensures that other customers are protected.  In 
contrast, creating a new class of service where transmission costs are not paid, particularly one 
that exempts those customers for either paying for services or simply for reliance on the shared 
system, does not ensure equitable treatment of other customers on the system.
